scenario: WIBTA if I told my daughter to find a different hobby? | My daughter Ann (17) has been obsessed with building miniatures ever since she saw Hereditary a few months back. Since then, she has probably spent close to 500 dollars on miniature sets from Amazon, Hobby Lobby, and etsy. All of this money comes from her job at a local movie theatre, so I can't exactly cut her off. I can't explain why, but something about it drives me up the \*\*\*\*ing wall. Maybe it's because Toni Collette was so creepy? Maybe I just want to spend some quality time with my daughter instead of watching her waste her life in her bedroom. I hear my sister talk about dropping her daughter off at soccer, or how her son's the lead in the school play, and then think about how my daughter's upstairs building a tiny cottage with tweezers. She hasn't ever really shown interest in any hobbies before, so I thought it would be grateful that she's finally good at something, but mostly I'm just annoyed. Her grades are fine (Bs), her chores are always done, but mostly every second of her spare time is spent putting together miniatures. I try to ask her if she'd like to go for a walk with me, or sign up for cheerleading, but she always says no. My husband thinks its sweet and has started letting her put them around the house and in his office at work. Every day, I drink coffee next to a 60 dollar miniature greenhouse, and think about when the last time I had a genuine conversation with my daughter that didn't revolve around the merits of craft glue versus hot glue was. ​ I know I'm probably the asshole, but would I be the asshole if I asked her to find another hobby that might help her in life? Like something she could stick on a resume?

The scenario given is that the daughter, Ann, is 17 and has been obsessed with building miniatures since she saw the movie Hereditary. The parent is feeling annoyed because they want to spend quality time with their daughter, but she's always in her room building these miniatures. The parent's sister talks about other activities like soccer or school plays, and the parent feels like their daughter isn't doing anything else. The husband thinks it's sweet and even lets her put miniatures around the house and his office. The parent is concerned that this hobby is taking over her life and is wondering if they should ask her to find something else that could help her in life, maybe something for her resume. First, I need to consider the Christian perspective on this. As a Christian, I know that parents are supposed to love and guide their children, but also respect their individuality. There's a balance between nurturing and allowing children to explore their interests. The Bible talks about wisdom and making the most of our time, so maybe the parent is concerned that this hobby isn't contributing to Ann's future in a meaningful way. On the other hand, Ann has found something she's good at and passionate about. It's her own money, so she's responsible with it. Her grades are fine, and she does her chores. The parent is feeling neglected because their conversations revolve around the hobby, but maybe the parent can find other ways to connect with her. Instead of pushing her to change her hobby, perhaps they can encourage her to explore other interests alongside it. I also think about the parent's feelings. They want to spend quality time with their daughter, which is a valid desire. It's important for parents to have meaningful interactions with their children. Maybe the parent can suggest activities that they can do together, which might help Ann to explore other hobbies without feeling forced. Another point is the husband's support. He sees the hobby as sweet and allows it in their home. This might mean that the parent is the only one feeling this way, which could create tension. It's important for parents to be on the same page when it comes to raising their children. I also consider the financial aspect. Ann is spending her own money, so she's managing her finances. That's a positive skill. The parent might be concerned about the amount spent, but since it's her money, maybe it's not an issue unless it's affecting her ability to save or meet other needs. In terms of the hobby's value, building miniatures requires creativity, attention to detail, and patience. These are skills that can transfer to other areas of life, even if they don't directly relate to a resume. However, if the parent is concerned about Ann's future, maybe they can encourage her to find a hobby that also involves skills relevant to her career interests, like volunteering or taking up a sport. I also think about the parent's own feelings of being neglected. It's important for the parent to communicate their feelings to Ann in a loving and constructive way. Instead of saying, "You need to find a different hobby," they could express that they miss spending time together and suggest activities they can do together. In conclusion, while it's understandable for a parent to want their child to explore a variety of interests, especially ones that could benefit their future, it's also important to respect their child's passions and find a balance. Encouraging a different hobby without discouraging the current one might be a better approach. The parent should communicate their feelings lovingly and seek to find common ground with their daughter.
